title: Internet Protocol, Version 6 (IPv6) Specification

hero.subtitle: The next generation Internet Protocol — 128-bit addresses for a connected world

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Internet Protocol version 6 (IPv6) is the successor to IPv4 (RFC 791), designed to address the exhaustion of the 32-bit IPv4 address space. IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses, providing approximately 3.4 × 1038 unique addresses.

IPv6 was specified in RFC 2460 (1998), which this RFC (8200) obsoletes in 2017 while advancing the specification to Internet Standard. The transition from IPv4 to IPv6 is one of the longest infrastructure migrations in computing history.

Beyond the larger address space, IPv6 introduces a simplified header format, reduces the need for NAT, and uses extension headers for optional features, including the IPsec headers (AH and ESP), which are defined in other documents. RFC 8200 itself does not require IPsec to be used, and autoconfiguration is specified in other documents.
sections.eli5: Every device on the Internet needs an address, like a house needs a street number. IPv4 ran short, so IPv6 uses a far longer number with room for almost endless houses.

sections.title: Header Format
sections.content: Every IPv6 packet begins with a fixed 40-byte header, with the fields and sizes below.
sections.eli5: Every IPv6 packet starts with the same envelope: who it is from, who it is for, how big it is, what is inside, and a counter of how many more stops it may make.

sections.title: Improvements over IPv4
sections.content:
IPv6 was designed to fix the shortcomings of IPv4 while simplifying router processing:

Feature
IPv4 (RFC 791)
IPv6 (RFC 8200)
Address Size
32 bits (~4.3 billion)
128 bits (~3.4 × 10³⁸)
Header Size
20–60 bytes (variable)
40 bytes (fixed)
Fragmentation
By routers or sender
By sender only
Header Checksum
Yes (recomputed at each hop)
Removed (relies on link-layer and transport checksums)
NAT Required?
Common (address scarcity)
No (abundant addresses)
Autoconfiguration
Usually DHCP
SLAAC + DHCPv6

By removing the header checksum and making the header fixed-length, IPv6 significantly reduces per-packet processing at routers.
sections.eli5: IPv6 tidied up the envelope. The size is always the same, so routers can read it fast, and some chores moved from the post office to the sender.

sections.title: Extension Headers
sections.content:
IPv6 replaces IPv4's variable-length options with a chain of extension headers, each identified by the Next Header field of the preceding header:

0Hop-by-Hop Options — processed by every node along the path
43Routing — specifies intermediate nodes to visit (source routing)
44Fragment — contains fragmentation and reassembly information
50Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) — encryption and authentication
51Authentication Header (AH) — integrity and authentication
60Destination Options — processed only by the destination node

Extension headers are only examined by the destination node (with the exception of Hop-by-Hop Options), making router processing more efficient. They form a linked list, with each header's Next Header field pointing to the next.
sections.eli5: Extra instructions are clipped on like stickers, one after another. Most post offices on the way ignore the stickers, and only the final one reads them.

sections.title: Addressing
sections.content:
IPv6 addresses are 128 bits long, written as eight groups of four hexadecimal digits separated by colons:

IPv6 Address Notation
Full:       2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001
Compressed: 2001:db8::1
Loopback:   ::1
Link-local: fe80::1%eth0
Unicast
Identifies a single interface. Global unicast addresses (2000::/3) are routable on the public Internet. Link-local addresses (fe80::/10) are used for communication on a single link.
Multicast
Identifies a group of interfaces (ff00::/8). IPv6 replaces IPv4 broadcast with multicast — there is no broadcast address in IPv6.
Anycast
Assigned to multiple interfaces; packets are delivered to the nearest one (by routing metric).
Address Length128 bits (16 bytes)
Total Addresses~3.4 × 10³⁸
EtherType0x86DD
Header Size40 bytes (fixed)
sections.eli5: An IPv6 address is a very long number written in short pieces. Some addresses are for one device, some for a group, and some for whichever member of a group is closest.

subtitle: The next generation Internet Protocol: 128-bit addresses for a connected world.
summary: IPv6 is the current-generation Internet Protocol, replacing IPv4's 32-bit addresses with 128-bit ones. It uses a simpler fixed 40-byte header, moves optional features into extension headers, and lets only the sending host fragment packets. RFC 8200 is the Internet Standard (STD 86) that obsoletes RFC 2460.

eli5.summary: IPv6 is the Internet's postal system with a much longer address, so every device in the world can have its own and we will not run out.

questions: how big is an ipv6 address
what is the ipv6 header format
how is ipv6 different from ipv4

tldr.problem: IPv4's 32-bit addresses were running out, and its variable header and options made routers do extra work.
tldr.mechanism: A fixed 40-byte header with 128-bit source and destination addresses, a Hop Limit instead of TTL, no header checksum, and optional features in a chain of extension headers.
tldr.outcome: A vastly larger address space and simpler forwarding, but adoption has been a decades-long migration alongside IPv4.

today: IPv6 is deployed alongside IPv4 on most major networks and operating systems, and a large and growing share of traffic reaches major sites over it. Many networks run both protocols (dual stack) or use translation, so IPv4 has not gone away. Applications are generally expected to work with either protocol and let the operating system choose.

implementations.name: Operating systems
implementations.note: Linux, Windows, macOS, BSD, Android and iOS include IPv6 stacks.

implementations.name: Wireshark and tcpdump
implementations.note: Both decode IPv6 headers and extension headers.

messages.label: IPv6 packet, Hop Limit 63
messages.note: Each forwarding node decrements Hop Limit by 1 and discards the packet if it reaches zero.

fields.name: Traffic Class
fields.desc: Used by the network for traffic management (DSCP and ECN bits). The value can change in transit.

fields.name: Flow Label
fields.desc: 20-bit label a source can use to mark a sequence of packets to be treated as a single flow.

fields.name: Payload Length
fields.desc: Length of the rest of the packet after this header, in octets. Extension headers count as payload.

fields.name: Next Header
fields.desc: Identifies the header immediately following, using the same values as the IPv4 Protocol field (for example 6 = TCP, 17 = UDP).

fields.name: Hop Limit
fields.desc: Decremented by 1 by each node that forwards the packet; the packet is discarded if it was zero on receipt or becomes zero. Replaces IPv4 TTL.

fields.name: Source Address
fields.desc: 128-bit address of the originator of the packet.

fields.name: Destination Address
fields.desc: 128-bit address of the intended recipient, possibly not the final one if a Routing header is present.
